abstract: THIS ARTICLE DESCRIBES THE DESIGN, construction, and testing of a 10-kVA three-phase to three-phase matrix converter induction motor drive. The converter has been built using discrete 65 A metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) controlled thyristors (MCTs). The commutation time has been minimized to avoid any unnecessary waveform distortion, particularly at low demanded output voltages. This minimization gives the matrix converter superior waveform quality in comparison to a conventional inverter and maximizes the available converter output voltage before overmodulation is required. The converter is vector controlled and has been tested using a 12-hp induction motor. Full results of these tests are presented.

SWITCHED RELUCTANCE MACHINES (SRMs) have gained momentum in the highly competitive market of adjustable speed motor drives. Owing to their rugged structure, simple geometry, and robust performance, SRM drives have made a successful entrance into various sectors of industry such as aerospace, automotive, and home appliances. In particular, the absence of magnetic sources on the rotor has turned SRM into a viable solution for applications in which operation under hostile ambient conditions is demanded.

THE TOTAL POWER DRAWN BY ELECTRIC LOADS ON TOP-CLASS vehicles today is settled around 2 kW, but it will soon overcome the threshold of 5 kW with the scheduled massive introduction of active suspension and drive-by-wire systems, as well as of several electric and electromechanical devices devoted to engine control and drive safety. Any action aimed to reduce fuel consumption and pollution emission on next-generation vehicles will require more electric power. Specifically, noticeable reductions of fuel consumption and pollution will be obtained by electrification of auxiliary mechanical drives that today are directly or indirectly powered by the engine shaft. Electrification will increase the efficiency of such systems that, when disconnected from the engine shaft, can be more rationally housed in the vehicle but not necessarily placed close to the engine. In addition, their operation can be made independent from the engine speed, achieving a greater flexibility. Some pioneering high-efficiency vehicles that have recently been introduced into the market feature a small electric propulsion system connected in parallel to the conventional internal combustion engine according to the so-called mild hybrid vehicle approach. Such an auxiliary propulsion system acts as an integrated starter generator (ISG) and supports or replaces the internal combustion engine in low efficiency operational conditions (stop-and-go driving, accelerations, light loads, load peaks, etc.) while allowing regenerative braking [1]—[5].

A SERIES OF IEEE 112A PERFORMANCE tests were conducted in 1999 and 2000 by Motor Systems Resource Facility (MSRF), Oregon State University, Corvallis, Oregon. The results of those tests were reported in a paper presented in June 2001 at the IEEE/IAS Pulp and Paper Industry Committee (PPIC) Technical Conference in Portland, Oregon. This article suggests a similar series of performance tests for variable speed drive (VSD) systems. Most applications for VSD systems involve variable torque loads—such as fans and centrifugal pumps—where the load power varies as the cube of the speed.

UNPLANNED INDUSTRIAL PROCESS DOWNTIME CAN BE VERY EXPENSIVE, frequently exceeding tens of thousands of dollars per hour. It is of crucial importance to utilize the plant downtime during planned maintenance periods for identifying all equipment that is likely to fail. Early identification of a weak motor and its replacement or repair during an outage is typically very inexpensive compared to the costs of plant downtime and rushed repairs.

WITH THE RAPID INCREASE OF adjustable speed drives (ASDs) in commercial and industrial facilities, the susceptibility of ASDs for power disturbances such as sags, swells, transients, and short-term power interruption has become an important issue. According to recent survey results, power interruption for 0.5 ≃ 5 s and voltage sags of 10% ≃ 40% below normal grid voltage for 3 ≃ 30 cycles are the majority of power disturbances caused to costly industry process disruption [2}. Although several studies concerning ride-through capability under power disturbances have been proposed [2], [3], [7], these studies have focused on three-phase pulsewidth modulation (PWM) rectifiers and/or PWM inverters.

INDUCTION MOTORS ARE THE most commonly employed electrical machines, in industry and elsewhere, throughout the world today. During its lifetime, an induction motor will convert such large quantities of energy that its “fuel bill” far exceeds its “first cost.” Consequently, investment in the quality of a motor that enables a reduction of its losses even by only a small percent that is frequently neglected is usually a financially sound practice. When examining the losses of an induction machine, it is possible to precisely identify the so-called “conventional losses,” which include stator and rotor conductor losses, magnetic core loss, and friction and windage loss. However, induction motors also have an additional power loss component termed “stray load loss” (SLL) that is caused by the nonideal nature of a practical machine. Also, because the SLL represents a small fraction of the total power, it is very difficult to calculate analytically. SLL has many components, and direct measurement is a very involved process. This has led to the adoption of allocations for SLL in efficiency standards. Unfortunately, many of the standards employed in manufacturing nations make different allocations for SLL. In an era of global commodity manufacturing, this makes for a difficult comparison of products. Usually, SLL can be evaluated by special experimental methods. Thus, one of the reasons for the differences in efficiency values from different national standards is the variation of SLL evaluation methods. However, SLL is a very significant part of overall losses that may have a big influence on the temperature situation of the motor. For some motors, the level of SLL can reach several percent of the input power and can seriously affect the efficiency. All of the above reasons make the evaluation of SLL in induction motors an important part of the efficiency estimation process. The use of calorimetry to precisely determine SLL is being pursued in several laboratories worldwide.

SINCE SHUNT ACTIVE POWER filters operate as controlled current sources injecting current harmonic components to the power distribution system, the point of connection must be carefully selected so the generated harmonic components flow to the nonlinear loads and do not propagate through the distribution system. In this article a numerical analysis based on analytical formulation that uses the power distribution system voltage and current transfer matrices is derived providing a user friendly and general tool to determine the most adequate point of connection for shunt active filters, improving the compensation effectiveness. Moreover, the proposed method allows the technical evaluation of the shunt active compensation in all the power distribution system. The validity of the developed method is verified by theory and computer simulation. Application to a real multibus power distribution system is presented.

MOST OF THE EXISTING HARMONIC MITIGATION SCHEMES FOR three-phase, four-wire systems focus on redirecting zero-sequence current harmonics from the neutral conductor back to the phase conductors. However, the portion of the neutral conductor that lies between the loads and the active filter is still burdened by the excessive current harmonics. In this article, a series active filter system for three-phase, four-wire distribution systems will be proposed. An active filter inverter will be placed in series connection with the neutral conductor to suppress the excessive current harmonics, thus preventing the overloading problem of the neutral conductor and the distribution transformer. Detailed analysis of the proposed system will be presented, and laboratory test results will be provided to validate the filtering performance of the proposed system.

OVER HALF OF NORTH-AMERICAN INDUSTRIES ARE EXPERIENCING EVEN greater requirements for up-time and reliability while reducing maintenance costs and scheduled outages. We often find that, in today's market, preventive maintenance and testing of electrical distribution equipment has been extended well beyond historical time periods or those recommended by the original equipment manufacturers. One method to address increasing up-time while reducing maintenance outages and costs is to perform more online predictive diagnostics. A well-known, traditional online predictive tool has been the thermograph survey. Thermography observes temperature, or hotspots, in the line of sight of the instrument. Partial-discharge (PD) analysis is the newest technology being applied to medium-voltage (MV) electrical equipment, and, in contrast to a thermograph, it can detect corona or surface tracking behind the metal barriers associated with MV equipment.

Optimization of electrostatic separation processes demands the control of a multitude of factors, including the characteristics of the granular mixtures to be sorted, the feed rate, the configuration of the electrode system, the applied high-voltage, and the environmental conditions. This article demonstrates that Taguchi's methodology of experimental design can be successfully employed for deriving a mathematical model capable of reflecting the effects of a large number of such factors, as well as their main interactions. The discussion of the results points out the main limitation of this technique: it neglects some interactions that might be nevertheless relevant to the process.

VARIABLE-SPEED DRIVES (VSDs) ARE KNOWN TO BE VULNERABLE TO voltage sags. These sags result in a reduced dc bus voltage that may cause torque or speed fluctuations or even a total shutdown of the drive and, consequently, of the production unit. Embedded solutions to improve the reliability of a VSD under voltage sag conditions have been investigated on a theoretical basis and are becoming commercially available. However, two important issues that have not been given much attention to in literature so far should be addressed before installing one of these solutions. First, the installation of mitigation equipment should be subject to a cost-benefit analysis. This is not trivial since both installation costs and benefits depend on the immunity level of the solution. Second, the consumers must have full confidence in the equipment, which can be obtained using practical measurements.

IN 1965, MAJOR BLACKOUTS IN the Northeast spurred the need to establish a council to create standards to help ensure the reliability of the bulk power generated in North America. This commission, the North American Electric Reliability Council (NERC), represents ten regions in the United States (Figure 1).

FLOATING, PRODUCTION, STORAGE, AND offloading (FPSO) systems are an alternative to other types of deep-water development and production systems such as spar platforms, tension leg platforms, and semi-submersible production systems. A large FPSO vessel may produce up to 300,000 barrels of oil per day (BOPD) and/or 600 million standard cubic feet of gas per day (SCFGPD), with two million barrels or more of on-board oil storage. Oil is normally off loaded by shuttle tanker and associated gas and produced water are normally injected to maintain field pressure. These vessels typically have more extensive electrical systems than the typical fixed platforms. Electrical operating loads may total 40–50 MW or more depending on the vessel configuration. Selection of the large drivers (turbines versus motors), picking the generation configuration (including prime, essential, and emergency), configuring the electrical distribution system, and locating the various parts of the electrical distribution system (hull versus topsides) are major critical early decisions that will impact the future coordination efforts of the project. This article will explore the design of various electrical systems and installation issues of typical FPSOs and provide some lessons learned.

articleTitle: A looming crisis? [HV engineering skills competency]
abstract: PETROCHEMICAL AND OTHER industrial and commercial facilities depend on continuous and reliable electric power. Although there is much focus on their hardware, there has been little attention given to avoidable errors in operation of industrial power systems. These errors have personnel and process safety, process uptime, and operating/maintenance cost implications. This article addresses an analysis of electric power disruptions from “inside the fence” causes over a four-year period in the global operations of a large chemical company. The underlying causes suggest problems in maintaining knowledge, skills, and experience in engineering, technical, and risk-management disciplines essential to power system operations. The authors have surveyed other large industrial companies to validate these findings and to project trends that could impact our industry.

articleTitle: William D. Coolidge and ductile tungsten
abstract: In May 1910, William D. Coolidge presented a significant paper concerning the discovery of a new method of producing ductile tungsten at a meeting of the American Institute of Electrical Engineers (AIEE). The breakthrough that he reported had been achieved by a research team led by Coolidge at the General Electric (GE) Laboratory in Schenectady, New York, and it was to have a major impact on production of electric lights, electronic tubes, and numerous other applications.

Electronic systems are continuously being developed to provide improved industrial productivity and reliability. As each generation of products evolves, it is promptly adopted by industry, with the promise of higher productivity, greater reliability, and lower production costs.

Advances in digital technology have provided relay designers with the tools to increase the capabilities of modern generator relays. This allows more sophisticated protection functions to be added to digital relays to provide better generator protection within a single relay hardware platform. Functions such as field-ground fault detection and brush lift-off detection are two examples of such relay functions. This article discusses field-ground protection using an injection method recently incorporated into a multifunction digital generator relay. The scheme presented in this article addresses field-ground detection on generators with brushes and an external source of dc field current and voltage. It has been installed on over 150 generators. Though many of today's new generators are brushless, there still exists a large population of older generators where the scheme described in this article is applicable. Developed and used in Europe for many years, the scheme lends itself to digital technology and offers many advantages over currently used field-ground dc voltage methods.

THROUGHOUT THE 20TH CENTURY, electrification became the most important engineering achievement, according to the U.S. National Academy of Engineering. Power generation and distribution, communication, heating, lighting, and control systems are examples of the industrial domains that were transformed by electrification. However, electrification has had the negative attribute of exposing people to potential injury and property loss from electrical hazards. Dramatic inventions and more uses in electrical technology have come at the expense of many lives and limbs [1].

articleTitle: Look up, look out for electrical safety!
abstract: What is the greatest opportunity for reducing workplace electrocutions? First reference point: I just returned from Washington, DC, where two of my IAS colleagues, Mary Capelli-Schellpfeffer and David Pace, and I spent the afternoon interviewing David Wallis, the director of Engineering Safety for the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Agency (OSHA), for a presentation at the 2004 IAS Electrical Safety Workshop. When asked about the greatest opportunity in reducing workplace-related electrical fatalities, he identified the prevention of unintentional contact with overhead power lines.

William Stanley, Jr. pioneered in the development and use of ac for electric light and HHHMB power applications. He conceived solutions before others recognized the problems. He contributed in a major way to a major invention: the transformer, the key to large-scale exploitation of ac electricity. Prior to 1885, few people were interested in ac except as a way to circumvent problems with sparking commutators on rotating electric machines. In March 1886, Stanley demonstrated a system of single-phase ac for lighting applications in Great Barrington, Massachusetts that changed the worldview of electricity. His system showcased the transformer which he invented two years prior. For the first time, this demonstration of long-distance, step-up/step-down, ac power transmission brought into public view the significant benefits offered by ac over dc [1]. Stanley led the way as engineers worldwide extended power transmission to ever-larger blocks of power, higher potentials, and increasing distances. He also invented a novel inductor electric machine that, during the last decade of the 19th century, was popular for use in power-generation applications. Starting in 1900, others began to adapt his inductor alternator to a wider range of applications; including radio broadcast, induction heating, and later, automotive electrical systems.

Greetings to my colleagues in the IAS! I am honored to have been appointed the IAS Standards Department chair at the beginning of 2004. I am a member of the IAS, PES, and IES. I started my involvement in IEEE in 1998 in the Industrial and Commercial Power Systems Department. The professional growth that I have experienced as a result of my participation in the society has widely exceeded my expectations. I have a passion for the mission of the Society. I am convinced that with this rich network of talented individuals, we can accomplish great things together. I would like to extend an invitation to all members to contact me with your concerns and ideas regarding standards activities.

No, not the robots in some Jurassic Park knockoff. I'm talking about some of the oddities of electrical apparatus that have come and gone within the memory of living engineers. These devices once represented the state of the art in their fields but have long ago been supplanted by more modern technology and apparatus that accomplishes the same ends. Some of these devices may still be in use in odd corners of the world, but few present-day electrical engineers have knowledge of them. This article describes a couple of these old technologies with which the author had personal experience. These descriptions are not as scholarly or well documented as most of the articles that appear in this space but are more of a memoir.

DIMMABLE ELECTRONIC BALLASTS ARE USED MORE AND MORE IN applications to reduce energy consumption by dimming or switching off artificial light in case of sufficient natural light. Another important reason for using a dim-mable ballast is to provide suitable lighting for the workplace. To define the requirements of an electronic ballast for such applications, we have to consider, on the one hand, the arrangement of the lighting system and, on the other hand, the signals used to control the dimming level.

THE NATIONAL ELECTRICAL CODE (NEC) governs all electrical installations in industrial facilities as well as commercial and residential occupancies. Since new products and electrical technology are constantly evolving, it is necessary to periodically revise the NEC to incorporate these changes in products and applications. This article defines the complete revision cycle and provides guidance for submitting proposals and comments to change the NEC.

I just picked up a copy of Fortune Magazine's annual issue featuring “The 100 Best Companies to Work For.” The J.M. Smuckers Co. in Orrville, Ohio, has taken first place in this annual survey; the co-CEOs are brothers and members of the Smuckers family. Their simple code of conduct (set forth by their father) is to: 1) listen with your full attention 2) look for the good in others 3) have a sense of humor 4) say “Thank You” for a job well done. Certainly, this is not rocket science, but the employees obviously appreciate being appreciated! Smuckers Director of Operations Brian Kinsey, who spent ten years at Proctor & Gamble says, “At first I was skeptical, but this family feel is for real.”

articleTitle: An interview with David Wallis, U.S. Osha director
abstract: Earlier this year, two IAS colleagues, Dr. Mary Capelli-Schellpfeffer, and David Pace and I spent an afternoon interviewing David Wallis, the Director of Engineering Safety for the U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Agency (OSHA). This government agency is responsible for establishing regulations for worker safety. We videotaped the interview for presentation at the 2004 IAS Electrical Safety Workshop held in February in Oakland, California, and we present excerpts from the interview in this issue. For information on how to obtain a videotape of the interview, go to http://ewh.ieee.org/cmte/ias-esw/and select “Archives”.

IN WEB/STRIP PROCESSING LINES, a popular control practice is to use torque/current regulators to set web/strip tension. In other applications, such as automotive test stands, a fast responsive torque regulator is required. This article provides guidelines for the useful interpretation of ac/dc torque/current performance specifications in these applications, from a drive system's application perspective.
For 88 years, high on a bluff overlooking Ardmore Boulevard in Forest Hills, Pennsylvania, an exceptional building stood. It is now in the last stages of demolition.

CURRENTLY, THERE ARE NO specific standards to distinguish premium-efficiency transformers from standard-efficiency transformers. The National Electrical Manufacturers Association (NEMA) has promulgated performance and test requirements for low-voltage designs that can be listed as NEMA Class I, and for such units efficiencies are somewhat higher than those that appear in the literature as standard designs. The U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), acting as required by the Energy Policy Act of 1992, is analyzing potential mandatory efficiency standards for a range of product classes that include the 500—2,500 kVA dry and liquid-type low-voltage transformers that are normally used in industrial substations. This article explores the practical economic effects of transformer selection over a range of efficiency levels at and above the NEMA Class I levels.

BEARING CURRENTS IN INDUCTION motors can result in premature bearing failure. In across-the-line driven electric motors, current-related bearing failures can occur due to a flow of current that is internally generated in the motor. The increased use of variable speed drives in industrial and commercial electric motor systems has raised the awareness of users as to a new source of bearing current flow that is externally sourced due to the switching characteristics of the inverter power source. Current paths within the motor and throughout the inverter-driven motor system must be well understood in order to apply effective bearing current remediation methods for these types of applications.

THERE IS A CONTINUOUS DEBATE today concerning the “motor of the future” for low-power applications requiring less than 1—2 kW. The specialists are focusing on superior motors [1] like brushless-dc, permanent-magnet synchronous, or electronically commutated types, because they show improvements in efficiency, reliability, torque-per-volume/mass ratio, maintenance, and service life. Despite this effort, the industry seems to be responding with manifest rigidity in changing standard induction motor solutions when considering the installed volume into the field, the investment in manufacturing base, and the easiness of transition from fixed speed to variable speed.

POWER ELECTRONICS REMAINS AN emerging technology. New materials, new devices, and new circuit topologies reduce the cost, weight, and volume for important applications [1]. Two important factors in power electronic circuits are the switching speed of the devices and the total power losses in the system. If the switching speed can be increased, improvements may be possible (e.g., current ripple in an electrical machine or physical size of passive components may be reduced). On the other hand, increased switching speed may cause additional losses in a power electronic system and increase the system cooling requirement. A common problem is that high-frequency phenomena like proximity effect, skin effect, hysteresis losses, and eddy current losses appear in the systems. These losses are very difficult to treat both theoretically and in practice. It is often difficult to measure the effect of increasing the switching frequency electrically because the system efficiency is high and a pure input-output measurement gives an unsatisfactory resolution and accuracy.

THE DESIGN OF POWER ELECTRONICS systems involves a large number of design variables and the application of knowledge from several different engineering fields (electrical, magnetic, thermal, and mechanical). In order to simplify the design problem, traditional design procedures fix a subset of the design variables and introduce assumptions (simplifications) based on the designer's understanding of the problem. These simplifications allow an initial design to be obtained in a reasonable amount of time, but further iterations through hardware prototype testing are usually required. The ability and expertise of the designer usually lead to good but not optimum designs.

OVER THE PAST FEW YEARS, INDUSTRIAL MANUFACTURING DISCIPLINES have evolved from a strategy of routine scheduled maintenance of electrical equipment to condition-based maintenance (CBM). In the CBM approach, equipment maintenance based on a routine schedule can be replaced with an approach based on system wellness diagnostics. This approach might rely on noninvasive monitoring of three-phase induction motors to report equipment condition and enable maintenance intervention before a failure occurs. Recent research conducted at Georgia Institute of Technology and the Eaton Innovation Center in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, has been conducted developing algorithms of motor current signature analysis (CSA) and power signature analysis (PSA), resulting in a reliable model to predict motor and driven load failure. Pump cavitation, rotational unbalance and mechanical alignment are some of the areas where a mathematical model has been developed using fast Fourier transform (FFT) analysis, enabling online diagnostics during operation. An extensive testing program to validate and refine the mathematical model was conducted both in the test lab and in field process applications. A "motor-wellness relay " is under development in a mechanical package designed to replace a conventional thermal-overload relay of a National Electric Manufacturing Association (NEMA) or Internacional Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) rated motor starter. With this approach, the online motor-wellness relay enables CBM via a control device that is already required for the control circuit. This article discusses the mathematical model and field tests to validate the model and introduce a motor-wellness relay chat could be used to perform online diagnostics. Alternative system communication architectures to support a wellness platform are also reviewed and discussed.

UNTIL RECENTLY, SILICON-CONtrolled rectifier (SCR) based, line-commutated ac power converters such as cycloconverters have dominated the field of megawatt-level, high-power, high-performance power conversion applications that require full regenerative capability. The advent of high-power, low-loss and fast switching devices such as high-voltage insulated gate bipolar transistors (IGBTs), integrated gate commutated thyristors (IGCTs), injection-enhanced gate transistors (IEGTs), and emitter turn-off (ETO) thyristors, have made it possible to build a high-power, high-performance, fully regenerative ac converter using a back-to-back pulsewidth-modulated (PWM) voltage source inverter (VSI) topology. Compared with cycloconverters and other line-commutated converters, the PWM VSIs have wider frequency range, faster dynamics, lower harmonics, higher power factor and, therefore, require little or no additional var compensation and bulky harmonic filters. As the dc link provides an energy buffer and decoupling between the ac input and output, ac converters based on PWM VSIs also have a better ride-through capability against ac line transients and can actually provide power-conditioning function to the ac grid.

Data are not available on how often arc faults occur in electrical equipment. These events are generally assumed to be of low frequency over the experience of all installations. However, when an arc fault does occur, the consequences are both severe and expensive with respect to: □ the personnel in the vicinity of the arc fault energy [1] □ the equipment involved in the arc fault □ the plant organization that responds to the consequences of the injuries and damage.

IN THE PAST, THE DECISION WHETHER TO REPAIR OR REPLACE AN electric motor has been one of economics. Replacement of an older electric motor with a more efficient model often makes sense for a motor operating continuously. However, in most cases, the decision is more complex (Figure 1) than the oft-cited “Replace the motor if repair cost exceeds x% of new.” When the cost of downtime is measured in tens of thousands of dollars, and delivery of a replacement motor is weeks away, rational thought replaces purchasing guidelines.

MANY PAPER MILLS AND OTHER industries use generators to supply critical process steam and electrical generation needs within the plant. The loss of a generating unit for an extended period would result in very costly replacement power and repair costs for any paper mill. As machine insulation systems age over decades, aging mechanisms progress to increase the risk of a possible ground fault internal to the generator. An IEEE/IAS Working Group Report [1]—[4] presenting methods of protecting medium-voltage industrial generators against extensive core and coil damage from internal ground faults was presented at the 2002 IEEE/IAS Annual Meeting and also at the 2003 Annual Pulp and Paper Industry Technical Conference. The report is comprised of four technical papers.

THIS ARTICLE DISCUSSES THE RELEVANCE OF STANDARDS in a global marketplace. In addition, it outlines the methods used by the IEEE and the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) standards process as well as the rules for standards development, including the procedures required to bring a standard to publication.

Electrical incidents do not have to result in injury or death. Every health effect, including death, amputation, burn, crush, blast, blindness, hearing loss and brain injury, is unnecessary. Engineering, scientific, and record-keeping experience over the last ten years has shown that electrical incidents are not random or rare. Safety professionals and electrical safety leaders are uniquely positioned to respond to every unintentional workplace exposure to electrical energy as a potentially fatal or environmentally threatening scenario. To enhance the fund of knowledge and resources available for professionals implementing safe electrical work practices, we present a historical overview of electrification and electrical safety management, followed by a survey of recent developments to reduce the frequency and severity of electrical incidents and their consequences. In the worlds of business, manufacturing, engineering, behavioral safety, and regulatory compliance, the financial case for improving electrical safety can be justified through measurable improvement by preventing injury to people, minimizing energy and raw materials waste, preventing process safety and environmental incidents, protecting capital investment from damage, and increasing uptime of operations.

articleTitle: Ballast-on-a-chip: realistic expectation or technical delusion
abstract: INTEGRATED CIRCUITS WILL, IN THE the future, play a greater role in electronic ballasts. At a panel session at the IAS 1999 Annual Meeting in Phoenix, Arizona, specialists from six leading ballast companies discussed the feasibility and suitability of silicon integration for electronic ballasts (1999 IEEE IAS Annual Meeting, Lighting Technical Sessions, Discussion Session, 6 October, Francis P. Dawson, University of Toronto, Canada, technical committee program chair). The discussion was led by Matthias Radecker, Fraunhofer-Institut IMS Duisburg, Germany. The discussion, even if partly commercial, gave a good overview about the complex challenges in this field. Following the panelists' suggestions, in this article, we present their original statements and figures. This is not meant to be advertising but demonstrates how concepts depend on the company's philosophy. One cannot completely realize where ballast silicon integration could lead us.

articleTitle: To test or not to test?
abstract: WHEN NEW MOTORS ARE PURCHASED, VARIOUS TESTS ARE CONDUCTED to verify performance and integrity. Many of these tests are not standardized and may add to the motor cost without adding significant value to the customer. Furthermore, while some of these tests may help ascertain a motor's reliability and performance, the testing may be harsh on the motor, degrading the integrity of the motor in the process. The value of the tests depends on the application, user experience, motor size/voltage, etc. By determining which tests are truly required, both from a cost and a harshness perspective, an optimized motor test can be purchased. Additionally, alternate test procedures may exist that may yield similar information without the stress imposed by more traditional test methods/specifications. This article will explore tests available for various induction motors and analyze the stress on the motor and value of information derived.

articleTitle: Handling changes from divisions to zones
abstract: WHEN A NEW EDITION OF A technical standard is issued, “anxiety” can be noted among the technical community because the new standard can reveal new concepts, and sometimes it becomes necessary to change the way we work. When not just one but many new standards are issued, this really causes a significant impact.

articleTitle: The right mix of drivers and power generation
abstract: TRADITIONALLY, FIXED AND FLOATING OFFSHORE PRODUCTION facilities in the Gulf of Mexico have used gas turbines or engines for large mechanical drives while providing separate gas turbines or engines for power generation. An alternate approach using electric power for feeding all loads, including large mechanical drives, is gaining favor as the scope of Gulf of Mexico facilities increases. During the initial design of a facility, it is critical to understand the different options that are available with regard to the driver selection. These options include using gas turbines for power generation with the options of having large mechanical drives coupled to gas turbines (traditional method) or using gas turbines only for power generation and using all electric drives for the mechanical loads. The critical areas that need to be evaluated in making this driver selection decision are project specific and typically include life-cycle cost, capital expenses, space and weight limitations, and emissions. For the all-electric facilities, the use of fixed-versus variable-speed drivers is also considered to improve energy efficiencies and operability.

articleTitle: Don't get lost in GOST standards
abstract: PREFABRICATED ELECTRICAL SUBSTATION BUILDINGS WERE chosen for supplying power to the pipeline linking the oil-producing regions of the Caspian Sea to a new port facility on the Black Sea. All electrical equipment was required to be in compliance with the standards and regulations of the Russian Federation and Kazakhstan. This added to the complexity of the design, construction, commissioning and operation of the equipment and systems. In this article, the authors describe some of the difficulties that occurred and the solutions implemented when applying local regulations and in obtaining GOST-R and GOST-K certification from the Russian Federation and Kazakhstan.

IT IS RECOGNIZED THAT THE predominate technology for hazardous location motor control installations in the petrochemical industry is motor control centers in a climate-controlled and pressurized environment. However, there are applications where cost, available real estate, or schedule would require the investigation of alternative technology. This article focuses on installations where a switchrack should be considered. The information will provide the tools for the engineer to identify situations where a switchrack would provide an acceptable solution and to make an accurate comparison of the two technologies. Based on this analysis, the technology that best meet the needs of the project can be chosen.

Dear Editor, I took a look at my article published in the May/June magazine, “Handling the changes from Divisions to Zones,” and I agree that the production result was excellent! I hope it helps IEEE Industry Application Magazine on its mission to divulge practical applications not only to IEEE members, but also to all technicians around the world.

One of the most important functions of any organization is to effectively communicate with its members. The IAS has several vehicles for accomplishing this objective and continually looks for methods to improve this communication.

Dear Editor: Re: Marketplace of Ideas: Should Technical Colleges Train New Grads? Increasingly, industry is expecting potential employees to come out of engineering schools fully trained, requiring no additional training on the job. Is job training the responsibility of the university or of industry?

articleTitle: IAS annual meeting includes opportunities for students
abstract: I would like to encourage students to apply for the Myron Zucker Travel Program that is available for the 2004 IAS Annual Meeting to be held at The Westin Hotel in downtown Seattle, Washington. The travel program is available to any student pursuing a technical degree that is within the scope of the IAS. The application process can be conducted online by clicking on the Travel tab at the top of the conference Web site (http://ewh.ieee.org/soc/ias/ias2004/), then following the link to the Student Travel Program. There is also a link from the IEEE IAS home page (http://www.ewh.ieee.org/soc/ias/). The application deadline is approximately 90 days before the conference; however, please check the Web site for the exact cut-off date. The Web site also includes a description of the travel allowances. Applications will be reviewed promptly, and recipients will be notified as soon as possible so that travel arrangements can be made.

As I write this column, I see repeated reports of the abuse of power. CEO's and mutual-fund managers are abusing their power for personal gain. Sports figures and entertainment celebrities are abusing their power for personal satisfaction. Politicians are abusing their power for greed. abstract: Chapter meetings are a key element of IEEE Industry Application Society (IAS) membership activity. A typical chapter meeting may consist of a technical or professional presentation and/or a tour of an interesting academic or industrial facility. Generally, these meetings are held in the evening or at lunchtime and are often combined with a meal and social session. However, the German Joint Industry Applications, Power Electronics, and Industrial Electronics Societies (IA/PELS/IE) Chapter, along with the German Power Engineering Society (PES) chapter, decided to go not one, not two, but three better than that with its “mega meeting.” The mega meeting was held over three days, 12-14 May in Berlin, Germany, and hosted at four different locations. The locations were: the German Association for Electrical, Electronic and Information Technologies (VDE) Berlin office, Siemens AG Power Transmission and Distribution—High Voltage Division, Alstom Power Conversion GmbH—General Drives, and the Berlin University of Technology Electrical Engineering and Computer Science research laboratories. This meeting had everything: technical presentations on contemporary industrial and academic topics, facility and laboratory tours, and excellent social gatherings that showcased German hospitality. Also, a proportion of the meeting was devoted to chapter and membership activities with presentations from the leadership of IEEE Region 8, VDE, IAS, IES, PELS, PES and IEEE Region 8 Chapter representatives. As with all good chapter meetings, there were unlimited opportunities to network, socialize, and learn. The IEEE sister societies, Industry Applications, Power Electronics, Industrial Electronics, and Power Engineering, helped to support and promote this workshop. Organizing such an event was a significant undertaking, and recognition and thanks must be given to the IEEE German PES and IA/IE/PELS Chapters leadership, Siemens, Alstom, the Technical University of Berlin, and all participants that made this memorable and historical event possible. This historical IEEE intersociety workshop and technical meeting exceeded all expectations. The following is the meeting report submitted by Dr. Ing. Andrås Lelkes.

When I was a young boy, my father, who lived his life in the Blue Ridge Mountains in rural Virginia, told me this story about his father. During the 1930s, my grandfather worked on the construction of the Blue Ridge Parkway, a scenic highway through the mountains of Virginia and North Carolina. One day, my grandfather was walking with a coworker through the construction area when each simultaneously exclaimed, “Watch out! There's a snake!” My grandfather followed with, “That's the largest rattlesnake I’ve ever seen!” His coworker responded with, “That's not a rattlesnake, it's a copperhead snake!” Each man was convinced that he was right and the other wrong until they realized that each was pointing to a different snake. The common ground they did share was that poisonous snakes present a hazard. “The lesson in this true story,” explained my father, “is that facts are most useful when everyone involved share and understand the same set of facts. Because each man had a different set of facts, each was wrong and each was right at the same time.” I remember wondering how a person could be right and wrong at the same time. It was not until years later that I understood the true meaning of the lesson in this story.

Dear Editor: I wish to offer a suggestion for improving IEEE Industry Applications Magazine. Please dispense with the goofy article titles in the features section of the table of contents. Two weeks after Hurricane Isabel devastated our area of eastern Virginia, we were still in the recovery process; a number of areas were without electric power, and downed trees were everywhere. This storm was not particularly strong in terms of wind velocity. The water table was very high due to a wet summer, and the already-saturated tree roots had little resistance to the sustained winds of 60–70 mi/h. A number of houses were condemned, with trees penetrating the structure of the house; our family was fortunate in that we only lost a number of very large trees, any one of which could have sliced our house in two. The trees all fell away from the house, and they will probably be on the ground for a long time until the tree trimmers can begin to catch up. No deaths were reported in this immediate area, but Virginia attributed 28 deaths to the storm.

abstract: André Blondel was born in Chaumont on 26 August 1863. Graduating first in his class at the École des Ponts et Chaussées (School of Bridges and Roadways) in 1888, he was employed as an engineer by the Lighthouses and Beacons Service. Engaged as assistant to the director of the central Lighthouses and Beacons Service, he retired in 1927 as general first class inspector. He was appointed commander of the “Legion d'honneur” (the highest French distinction) in 1927 and life member of the French Academy of Science in 1913. He was honorary president of the French Electricians Society, in which he had been interested since 1890 and had enjoyed the privilege of his scientific communications.
